Question: are the differences between counties in the share of lung cancer patients who receive curative-intent treatment larger than chance alone would produce, and which counties are genuine outliers?

Do this:
1. Build a county table: patients (denominator), patients with curative-intent treatment, share. State exactly which rows you used; if counts are missing for a county, derive them from the share and the case count and say so.
2. Funnel plot: share against number of patients, with the national share as the centre line and 95% and 99.8% binomial control limits. Label counties outside the 95% limits. Test for overdispersion and, if present, also show overdispersion-adjusted limits.
3. Report which counties fall outside the limits (above and below), with their shares, counts and exact binomial p-values, and how many patients a year separate each low outlier from the national share.
4. Exploratory only: rank correlations of the county share with share of population aged 65+, daily smoking, education, distance to a university hospital and lung cancer incidence. Say clearly that with 22 or 23 counties these are ecological associations, not causes, and report confidence intervals.
5. State the limits: the registry itself says stage is recorded for about half of patients and recording practice differs by county, so part of the difference may be recording.

Outputs: the county table as CSV, the funnel plot as PNG (clear enough for a slide: readable labels, Finnish county names in English), a short results summary in Markdown, and the full analysis script. Use only numbers from the files; if something is missing, say so instead of substituting a value.

output_data.response:
**Yes — the between-county differences are far larger than chance.** Homogeneity test on the 22 counties with counts: Q = 187.7 on 21 df, p ≈ 10⁻²⁸, dispersion factor φ = 8.5 (winsorised 6.6), between-county SD τ = 4.9 pp. Shares run 18.5 % → 35.6 % around a national 27.0 %.

![Funnel plot of curative-intent treatment share by county]({{artifact:91f56a8b-8394-4d32-9078-13a98aee567d}})

**Rows used.** All 22 counties that carry both counts (`area_id` 01–21, 90). Åland (`area_id` 91) has patients, curative-intent count, share and case count all empty — nothing is derivable, so it is excluded everywhere, including the correlations. **No count had to be derived from share × case count:** `lung_cases_5y_n` equals `lung_patients_2019_2023_n` for all 22, and the recomputed shares reproduce the reported ones to ≤0.05 pp. The Finland row is used only as the centre line (4,009/14,873 = 26.95 %). The 22 counties sum to 14,774 patients and 3,992 treatments, so 99 patients and 17 treatments sit in the national total but in no county row; using the 22-county sum (27.02 %) as the centre line instead leaves the set of flagged counties unchanged.

**Outliers (exact two-sided binomial vs 26.95 %, BH q across 22 tests).**

| Above | n | treated | share | p | q |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Vantaa and Kerava | 595 | 212 | 35.6 % | 3.6e-06 | 2.6e-05 |
| Central Uusimaa | 481 | 162 | 33.7 % | 0.0012 | 0.0033 |
| Helsinki | 1,486 | 491 | 33.0 % | 2.2e-07 | 2.4e-06 |
| Pirkanmaa | 1,253 | 400 | 31.9 % | 1.0e-04 | 4.4e-04 |
| West Uusimaa | 1,058 | 337 | 31.9 % | 4.1e-04 | 0.0015 |

| Below | n | treated | share | p | q | shortfall, patients/yr |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Lapland | 710 | 131 | 18.5 % | 1.4e-07 | 2.4e-06 | 12.1 |
| South Karelia | 355 | 67 | 18.9 % | 5.0e-04 | 0.0016 | 5.7 |
| Kymenlaakso | 591 | 114 | 19.3 % | 1.6e-05 | 8.6e-05 | 9.1 |
| Kainuu | 226 | 47 | 20.8 % | 0.0359 | 0.0659 | 2.8 |
| North Karelia | 510 | 109 | 21.4 % | 0.0044 | 0.0107 | 5.7 |
| North Ostrobothnia | 1,050 | 248 | 23.6 % | 0.0149 | 0.0327 | 7.0 |
| Southwest Finland | 1,437 | 349 | 24.3 % | 0.0221 | 0.0442 | 7.7 |

All five high counties and Lapland, South Karelia, Kymenlaakso are outside the 99.8 % limits; the other four low counties are between the 95 % and 99.8 % limits, and Kainuu is the only one that loses significance after FDR adjustment (q = 0.066). Together the seven low counties are about **50 patients a year** short of the national share.

With limits inflated by √φ = 2.58, only Helsinki stays outside — the adjusted limits absorb the county-level spread into the null, so they test "unusual *given* that counties differ this much", not whether the counties differ. Vantaa and Kerava has the highest share but falls inside the adjusted band because its denominator is smaller than Helsinki's.

**Rank correlations (exploratory, n = 22, Spearman with Bonett–Wright CIs):** 65+ share ρ = −0.77 (−0.91, −0.47); distance to university hospital −0.66 (−0.86, −0.30); lung cancer incidence −0.62 (−0.84, −0.24); education index +0.49 (+0.06, +0.77); daily smoking −0.30 (−0.65, +0.15). These are ecological associations between county aggregates, not causes — the five variables are strongly intercorrelated, the CIs are wide at 22 units, and none of this identifies an effect on an individual patient's chance of curative-intent treatment.

**Limits.** The registry reports stage for roughly half of lung cancer patients with county-varying recording practice, so part of the spread is documentation rather than care. The `lung_no_treatment_record_pct` column supports that reading: it ranges 16.4 % to 43.1 %, and Southwest Finland (43.1 %) and South Karelia (42.8 %), both low-share counties, hold the two highest values. There is no case-mix adjustment available (no stage, performance status, histology or comorbidity in the table), cross-county referral to university hospitals can move counts between neighbours, and the five pooled years span COVID-19 with no annual breakdown. Full caveats are in §5 of the summary.

<skill-metadata name="figure-style" source="anthropic" note="read-only — fork under a new name to modify" />

# Publication-Grade Figure Rules

*A checklist for correct, legible, internally-consistent scientific figures. This
skill does not impose a visual house style — frame, font, and palette are
parameters. Once loaded, call `apply_figure_style()` before plotting.*

## §0 Scope

**Load trigger** (same rule as the system prompt's "Publication-grade plots"
section): this skill is for **final-deliverable figures** — those shipping in a
report, paper, or export, or saved as an artifact the user will keep — not for
exploratory/intermediate plots (quick looks, EDA, sanity checks), which are
drawn plainly without it. Once loaded, "every plot" below means every plot you
render toward the deliverable.

§1–§3, §8, and §9 are **correctness** — they apply to every plot, in every
context, and have no aesthetic content. §4–§7 are **guidance** — defaults that
produce a clean result but that a deliberate alternative can override
(individual rules inside §4–§7 that state a factual/perceptual invariant — e.g.
§4.4 semantic-zero centering, §4.5 CVD, §6.9 leader anchoring — still bind). On
its own, this skill is the inner tier (make one plot good); `figure-composer`
and `paper-narrative` supply multi-panel and whole-paper context.

---

## §1 Data fidelity & self-consistency

**1.1 Excluded rows.** A row marked excluded or flagged in the source data is
either omitted entirely or drawn with a visually distinct open/hatched marker
and named in the key. It **never** enters a summary statistic plotted alongside
the included rows.

**1.2 Comparable conditions only.** Arms measured under non-comparable
conditions (different N, epoch budget, initialization, protocol) are not plotted
as visual peers. Separate them with a facet break or a marker on the label, and
state the difference once in the caption.

**1.3 Self-consistency.** Every key, threshold, and title inside the figure must
be satisfied by every plotted row. Before saving, walk each categorical outcome
label back to the rule that defines it; if a row's value contradicts its label
or the title, the figure is wrong, not the data.

**1.4 Claim-titles must be true.** A sentence-title (§5.1) is tested against
every category on the axis before rendering. If any contradicts it, qualify the
title ("on 3 of 4 pairs") or downgrade it to a description.

**1.5 State n and what was held fixed.** Every panel that draws a summary mark
states `n` and the unit of replication, and every small-multiple that holds a
variable fixed states the fixed value — in the panel or, when §2 budget is
tight, in the caption.

**1.6 Reference structure is reference.** A tree, ordering, or topology drawn as
*context* (a scale bar, a category strip) uses an established reference, not
one inferred from the plotted data. Infer the structure only when the structure
*is* the result.

**1.7 One number per claim.** A quantitative claim (runtime, accuracy, count)
has exactly one canonical value across every panel, caption, and the abstract.
Define what it measures and use that value everywhere.

---

## §2 Label economy — floor and ceiling

The figure shows the pattern; the **caption** carries the context. Design for a
general scientific reader, not the author.

**2.1 Floor (non-removable).** Every distinct mark, series, glyph, or comparator
must be identifiable from the figure alone. The caption explains *why it
matters*, not *what it is*. A label is non-removable if deleting it leaves a
reader asking "what is that?"; it is removable only if the question becomes "why
is that there?". Comparator labels name the thing ("prior method", "no joint
training"), never a bare role word ("baseline", "previous"). Any term a general
scientist can't parse gets a one-word gloss.

**2.2 Ceiling.** Per panel: title + axis labels + tick labels + series identity
(labeled once per row of small multiples) + at most 2–3 result annotations.
Count the strings; >6 beyond axes/ticks means you're over. The ceiling counts
*narrative* annotations (callouts, value labels, brackets) — identity labels are
floor, not budget.

**2.3 Move to the caption:** n=, what's-held-fixed, abbreviation expansions,
non-comparable footnotes, exclusion rationale, methodological caveats.

**2.4 Titles are takeaways.** A reader seeing only the title knows what the
panel shows. "Robust to gene dropout" passes; "Fewer genes" fails. Test: read it
aloud cold — if the listener asks "fewer genes *what*?", rewrite. For a row of
small multiples that vary one thing, drop per-panel titles for one row-header.

**2.5 Value-on-mark only for the headline number** — the one a reader would
quote. Everything else is read off the axis.

**2.6 When in doubt, delete the label and re-read.** If the message survives, it
stays deleted.

---

## §3 Axes, scales, small multiples

**3.1 Axis padding.** Axis limits clear the data by ≥ one marker radius on every
side; markers and text never touch a spine. `ax.margins(0.04)` after plotting,
or extend the limit past any annotation.

**3.2 Axis breaks over wasted range.** When data occupy <40 % of an axis, break
the axis or start it at the data floor with a clear non-zero tick. Never draw a
reference line, threshold, or annotation inside a broken-axis gap — the gap has
no coordinate.

**3.3 Log axes get human-readable ticks** — `10²`, `10³`, or `1k / 10k / 100k`,
not raw exponents. **Never** draw filled bars on a log-scaled value axis (bar
length encodes ratio to an arbitrary floor); use points + median tick instead.

**3.4 Shared axes across small multiples.** A row or column of small multiples
shows tick labels once (leftmost / bottommost panel); interior panels keep ticks
but drop labels. When the panels share a y-axis and differ only by x-variable,
render them as abutting subplots (`wspace≤0.06`) with one row-header title.

**3.5 Fill the box.** A panel's data envelope occupies ≥75 % of its allotted
rectangle. If a panel's natural aspect leaves dead bands, reshape the grid
(rowspan, stacked complementary panels) — don't pad the panel.

**3.6 Direction of goodness.** When higher- or lower-is-better is not obvious
from the axis label, place a small upright cue ("higher = better") in the
margin — once per row of panels, never per panel, and never only in the caption.
A directional glyph embedded in rotated text rotates with it; set the cue
upright.

**3.7 Physical width.** A single-row figure at 300 dpi fits the venue's
double-column width. Adding a schematic or labels does not push data panels narrower than
they were before.

---

## §4 Color

**4.1 Threading.** Once a color is bound to an entity (a method, a feature, a
condition), reuse that exact color for every mark representing that entity
across the figure — line, fill, marker, text, heatmap row. Color *is* the
cross-reference; a reader should never have to consult a legend twice.

**4.2 Limit hues.** Use as few distinct hues as the data require. When the
figure compares a focal series against others, make the focal series visually
dominant (saturated, heavier weight) and render comparators with lower visual
weight (desaturated, lighter, or thinner). The focal hue must not coincide with
any hue in a categorical palette used in the same figure. The focal series must
remain identifiable even when its mark is zero-width or coincident with others —
via outline, marker, or a light tinted band.

**4.3 Hierarchical categories.** When categories nest (groups within groups),
the outer level picks the hue family and the inner level samples within it.

**4.4 Continuous and diverging.** Use a perceptually uniform sequential map for
generic continuous values; a single-hue ramp for ordinal rank or size; a
diverging map for signed quantities — **always** centered at the semantically
meaningful zero (0, 1.0, or median), never the data midpoint.

**4.5 CVD safety.** Never rely on a red/green contrast for a binary or opposing
distinction. Any binary pair should remain distinguishable in deuteranopia
simulation. Reserve one alarm hue for error/anomaly/perturbation marks and do
not reuse it as a data-series color.

**4.6 Two palettes, two legends.** When a figure uses two categorical color
systems, each legend sits adjacent to the first panel where its palette applies.

---

## §5 Typography

**5.1 Sentence titles.** A panel title states the comparison in plain language,
regular weight, left-aligned. Metric names go on the axis, not in the title.

**5.2 Role-mapped size ladder.** A figure uses **at most three** font sizes,
mapped to *role* not space: titles/axis-labels/series-identity at the base size;
legend/annotation text one step down; tick labels one step further. Panel
letters are the only exception (bold, larger). If a label doesn't fit at its
role's size, fix the layout or shorten the text — don't reach for an
intermediate size. `apply_figure_style(sizes=(8,7,6))` sets the ladder.

**5.3 Nomenclature.** Species, gene, and variable names that scientific
convention italicizes are italicized. Abbreviated codes inherit the rule; expand
once on first appearance.

**5.4 Magnitude suffixes.** Large counts use `k / M / B` (`4.2B`, `120 kb`),
not comma-grouped full numerals.

**5.5 Numeric annotations.** On-mark numbers use at most 2 significant figures —
unless 2-sf rounding would make two distinct rows print the same value, in which
case show the digit that separates them. Text on a filled mark reaches ≥4.5:1
contrast; if it doesn't, place the text outside the mark.

**5.6 No internal codes.** Axis labels use plain-language names; codebase
abbreviations appear only in parentheses after the readable name or in the
caption. Comparator series are labeled with what they *are*, not a role word.

**5.7 Panel letters.** Bold, top-left, outside the axes box. Case follows the
target venue's convention; `panel_letter(ax, 'a', case=...)` handles either.

---

## §6 Chart-family guidance (by data shape)

**6.1 Categorical × numeric.** Show the distribution, not just the summary.
Chart choice follows n: jittered strip with a median tick for small n; box or
violin for large n; bar + overlaid raw points or bar + interval when the mean is
the message. The `errorbar='ci95'` interval is the t-distribution 95% CI of the
mean (half-width `t_{0.975,n−1}·s/√n`), so it is valid at small n. Error bars
and raw-point overlays are alternatives — showing both is usually redundant. A
category absent from a group is marked (`n.d.`, `—`, or a hatched ghost) at its
slot; an empty slot reads as zero. A zero-valued bar
gets a visible stub or dot at the baseline.

**6.2 Single-observation categories.** A filled dot with a thin neutral stem to
the semantic zero (lollipop). Value labels sit beside the dot.

**6.3 Continuous series.** Mean-per-x as a line with markers; individual runs as
thin translucent lines or points behind it. Label each series with direct text
at the right end of its line in preference to a legend box. Summary glyphs
(per-bin mean/median) use a shape that cannot be mistaken for a raw observation,
identical across series, drawn below the raw points in z-order.

**6.4 Distributions on shared support.** When two distributions overlap heavily,
stack them as small panels with a shared x-axis or use a ridgeline. Overlay only
when the separation is visually clear.

**6.5 Matrices.** When a heatmap is small enough to read (< ~200 cells), print
the value in every cell. State the threshold once in the colorbar label.

**6.6 Embeddings.** Dimensionality-reduction scatters (UMAP, t-SNE, PCA) drop
ticks and tick labels; a small corner arrow pair names the axes. Clusters are
labeled by thin leader lines to text in surrounding whitespace.

**6.7 Paired prediction vs. observation.** Stack the two as adjacent tracks with
identical x and color; let the alignment carry the comparison. Target regions
are translucent spans registered in the legend.

**6.8 Insets.** Connect a detail inset to its source region visibly — a bounding
box with connector lines, or a translucent wedge.

**6.9 Label the extremes.** On a scatter of named observations, direct-label at
least the maximum, minimum, and any flagged point with a thin leader line. After
rendering, verify every leader endpoint terminates within one marker radius of
the row it names.

---

## §7 Layout & narrative

**7.1 Show what is measured before the result.** A reader should grasp what's
being compared before seeing the comparison — via a plain-language title, a
labeled schematic, or panel ordering. Any schematic uses the same words and
glyphs as the data panels' labels.

**7.2 One figure, one message.** A multi-panel figure has a single sentence it
is trying to make true. Every panel either states it, supports it, or bounds it;
panels that do none of these belong in supplement.

**7.3 Legends live in whitespace.** Frameless, placed inside the figure's
natural whitespace, or replaced by direct labeling. Legend entries are
swatch-first, left-aligned, and resolve every visually distinct glyph on the
panel.

**7.4 Row-band headers for nested faceting.** When small multiples are grouped,
each group gets one spanning header, not repeated per-panel titles.

**7.5 The figure arc.** For a paper: Figure 1 renders the paper's one-sentence
pitch as data — scope, not architecture. Subsequent figures cover mechanism,
evidence, robustness, application. A panel is judged against the paper's pitch,
not just its own figure's claim; content moves between figures if that's where
the story needs it. (`paper-narrative` runs this review.)

**7.6 Don't re-decorate a passing panel.** Between revision rounds, a panel that
already passes is not made more visually complex to fix nothing. Adding marks or
labels to a clean panel is a regression.

---

## §8 Anti-patterns

These are correctness failures, not style preferences:

- Red and green as opposing categories.
- Filled bars on a log-scaled value axis.
- Colorbar ticks that are evenly spaced but miss the semantic center.
- A diverging colormap whose center is the data midpoint, not the semantic zero.
- An axis title that restates the tick labels.
- Explaining the direction of goodness only in the caption.
- A "reference" line drawn at a value that is itself one of the plotted points.
- An excluded row that enters a plotted summary statistic.
- A leader line whose nearest mark is not the row it labels.

---

## §9 Render-then-verify

After `fig.savefig(...)`, before `save_artifacts`:

**9.1 Geometric (bbox) check.**
```python
r = fig.canvas.get_renderer()
texts = [(t, t.get_window_extent(r)) for t in fig.findobj(mpl.text.Text)
         if t.get_text().strip() and t.get_visible()]
spines = [(s, s.get_window_extent(r)) for ax in fig.axes
          for s in ax.spines.values() if s.get_visible()]
ticklabels = {ax: set(ax.get_xticklabels(which='both') + ax.get_yticklabels(which='both'))
              for ax in fig.axes}
overlaps  = [(a, b) for i, (a, ba) in enumerate(texts) for b, bb in texts[i+1:] if ba.overlaps(bb)]
overlaps += [(t, s) for t, bt in texts for s, bs in spines
             if bt.overlaps(bs) and t not in ticklabels[s.axes]]
# assert: overlaps == [] and every text box lies within fig.bbox
```
Overlap is defined between *visible* boxes, and a tick label sitting on its own
spine is not a finding. Fix (move, shorten, stagger) and re-save until clean.

**9.2 Perceptual check.** The bbox check is geometric, not perceptual — it will
not catch a low-contrast label, a leader that crosses three others, or a series
color mistakable for another. Crop the saved PNG to each panel and look:
```python
fig.savefig("figure.png")
for letter, box in panel_crops(fig).items():
    host.view_image("figure.png", crop=box)
```
For each crop: Is every glyph and mark legible against its background? Does the
smallest plotted element have a stroke or stub? Do any leaders cross? Could any
series color be mistaken for another? Does the legend sit beside what it keys?
A perceptual defect that passes §9.1 is still a defect.

---
*When in doubt: fewer hues, more direct labels, raw data over summary stats, and
state what is being measured before showing the result.*

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Between-county variation in curative-intent treatment of lung cancer, Finland 2019-2023.

Input : county_table_input.csv  (Finnish Cancer Registry lung cancer quality report
        2019-2023 + Statistics Finland / THL Sotkanet context columns)
Output: county_table_analysis.csv
        funnel_curative_intent.png
        results_summary.md

Method: indirectly standardised-free proportion funnel plot (Spiegelhalter 2005),
exact binomial control limits with continuous interpolation, Spiegelhalter's
winsorised overdispersion factor phi, exact two-sided binomial tests per county,
Spearman rank correlations with Bonett-Wright confidence intervals.
No value is imputed; Aland has no counts and is excluded from all inference.
"""
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from scipy import stats, special, optimize
import matplotlib as mpl
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

ALPHA_IN, ALPHA_OUT = 0.05, 0.002          # 95 % and 99.8 % limits
YEARS = 5                                  # 2019-2023

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- 1. county table
raw = pd.read_csv("county_table_input.csv", dtype={"area_id": str})
nat = raw.loc[raw.area_id == "FI"].iloc[0]
cty = raw.loc[raw.area_id != "FI"].copy()

# the registry report gives patients and curative-intent counts directly; the second
# source's case count (lung_cases_5y_n) is identical for every county with data, so
# nothing has to be derived from share x case count.
agree = (cty.lung_cases_5y_n == cty.lung_patients_2019_2023_n)
assert agree[cty.lung_patients_2019_2023_n.notna()].all()

dat = cty.loc[cty.lung_patients_2019_2023_n.notna()].copy()     # 22 counties
excluded = cty.loc[cty.lung_patients_2019_2023_n.isna(), "county"].tolist()

dat["n"] = dat.lung_patients_2019_2023_n.astype(int)
dat["x"] = dat.curative_intent_n.astype(int)
dat["share_pct"] = 100 * dat.x / dat.n

p0 = nat.curative_intent_n / nat.lung_patients_2019_2023_n      # national centre line
n_sum, x_sum = dat.n.sum(), dat.x.sum()

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- 2. per-county tests
se = np.sqrt(p0 * (1 - p0) / dat.n)
dat["z"] = (dat.x / dat.n - p0) / se
dat["p_exact"] = [stats.binomtest(int(x), int(n), p0, alternative="two-sided").pvalue
                  for x, n in zip(dat.x, dat.n)]
ci = np.array([stats.binomtest(int(x), int(n), p0).proportion_ci(method="exact")
               for x, n in zip(dat.x, dat.n)])
dat["share_ci_low_pct"], dat["share_ci_high_pct"] = 100 * ci[:, 0], 100 * ci[:, 1]
rej, q, *_ = __import__("statsmodels.stats.multitest", fromlist=["x"]).multipletests(
    dat.p_exact, alpha=0.05, method="fdr_bh")
dat["p_exact_bh"] = q
# patients per year between the county and the national share (negative = shortfall)
dat["excess_treated_per_year"] = (dat.x - p0 * dat.n) / YEARS

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- 3. overdispersion
K = len(dat)
Q = float((dat.z ** 2).sum())                       # == Pearson chi-square on K-1 df
p_Q = stats.chi2.sf(Q, K - 1)
phi = Q / K

def winsorised_phi(z, frac=0.1):
    """Spiegelhalter (2005) eq. 32: winsorise the extreme `frac` of each tail of z."""
    lo, hi = np.quantile(z, [frac, 1 - frac])
    return float((np.clip(z, lo, hi) ** 2).mean())

phi_w = winsorised_phi(dat.z.values)
# additive (random-effects, DerSimonian-Laird) between-county SD on the share scale
tau2 = max(0.0, (Q - (K - 1)) / (np.sum(1 / se ** 2) - np.sum(1 / se ** 4) / np.sum(1 / se ** 2)))
tau_pct = 100 * np.sqrt(tau2)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- 4. control limits
def exact_limits(n_grid, p, alpha):
    """Exact binomial control limits with continuous interpolation in the count k:
    P(X<=k) = I_{1-p}(n-k, k+1) treated as a continuous function of k."""
    out = np.empty((len(n_grid), 2))
    for i, n in enumerate(n_grid):
        f = lambda k, targ: special.betainc(n - k, k + 1, 1 - p) - targ
        for j, targ in enumerate((alpha / 2, 1 - alpha / 2)):
            out[i, j] = optimize.brentq(f, 1e-9, n - 1e-9, args=(targ,)) / n
    return out[:, 0], out[:, 1]

ngrid = np.linspace(80, 1600, 400)
lo95, hi95 = exact_limits(ngrid, p0, ALPHA_IN)
lo998, hi998 = exact_limits(ngrid, p0, ALPHA_OUT)
infl = np.sqrt(phi_w)                                  # multiplicative inflation
adj = lambda lim: p0 + infl * (lim - p0)               # scale the limit's distance to p0

def flag(row):
    nn = row.n
    f = lambda a: exact_limits(np.array([nn]), p0, a)
    (l95, h95), (l998, h998) = f(ALPHA_IN), f(ALPHA_OUT)
    s = row.x / nn
    if s > adj(h998[0]) or s < adj(l998[0]): band = "outside 99.8% (overdisp-adj)"
    elif s > adj(h95[0]) or s < adj(l95[0]): band = "outside 95% (overdisp-adj)"
    elif s > h998[0] or s < l998[0]: band = "outside 99.8% (binomial only)"
    elif s > h95[0] or s < l95[0]: band = "outside 95% (binomial only)"
    else: band = "within 95%"
    return pd.Series({"limit_band": band,
                      "direction": "above" if s > p0 else "below",
                      "lcl95_pct": 100 * l95[0], "ucl95_pct": 100 * h95[0],
                      "lcl998_pct": 100 * l998[0], "ucl998_pct": 100 * h998[0],
                      "lcl95_adj_pct": 100 * adj(l95[0]), "ucl95_adj_pct": 100 * adj(h95[0]),
                      "lcl998_adj_pct": 100 * adj(l998[0]), "ucl998_adj_pct": 100 * adj(h998[0])})

dat = pd.concat([dat, dat.apply(flag, axis=1)], axis=1)
dat["outside95_binomial"] = ~dat.limit_band.eq("within 95%")
dat["outside95_adjusted"] = dat.limit_band.str.contains("adj")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- 5. funnel plot
import kernel as fs  # figure-style helpers (apply_figure_style, panel_crops, ...)
fs.apply_figure_style()
BLUE, RED, GREY = "#1f5fa9", "#c3272b", "#6e6e6e"

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.0, 5.6))
for y, ls, lw, c, lab in [(lo95, (0, (5, 3)), 1.1, GREY, "95 % limits (binomial)"),
                          (hi95, (0, (5, 3)), 1.1, GREY, None),
                          (lo998, (0, (1, 2)), 1.1, GREY, "99.8 % limits (binomial)"),
                          (hi998, (0, (1, 2)), 1.1, GREY, None)]:
    ax.plot(ngrid, 100 * y, ls=ls, lw=lw, color=c, label=lab, zorder=2)
ax.fill_between(ngrid, 100 * adj(lo95), 100 * adj(hi95), color=BLUE, alpha=.085,
                lw=0, label=f"95 % limits, overdispersion-adjusted ($\\phi$={phi_w:.1f})", zorder=1)
ax.plot(ngrid, 100 * adj(lo95), color=BLUE, lw=1.3, zorder=2)
ax.plot(ngrid, 100 * adj(hi95), color=BLUE, lw=1.3, zorder=2)
ax.axhline(100 * p0, color="k", lw=1.4, zorder=3,
           label=f"Finland {100*p0:.1f} %  ({int(nat.curative_intent_n):,}/{int(nat.lung_patients_2019_2023_n):,})")

ins, outs = dat[~dat.outside95_binomial], dat[dat.outside95_binomial]
ax.scatter(ins.n, ins.share_pct, s=46, color=BLUE, edgecolor="white", lw=.7, zorder=5)
ax.scatter(outs.n, outs.share_pct, s=74, color=RED, edgecolor="white", lw=.8,
           zorder=6, marker="D")

# direct labels for every county outside the 95 % binomial limits
off = {"Vantaa and Kerava": (0, 13), "Helsinki": (0, 12), "Pirkanmaa": (0, -15),
       "Southwest Finland": (0, -15), "Lapland": (0, -14), "Kymenlaakso": (0, 12),
       "South Karelia": (-6, -15), "North Ostrobothnia": (0, 13), "Satakunta": (0, -14),
       "West Uusimaa": (0, 12)}
for _, r in outs.iterrows():
    dx, dy = off.get(r.county, (0, 12))
    ax.annotate(f"{r.county}\n{r.share_pct:.1f} %", (r.n, r.share_pct),
                textcoords="offset points", xytext=(dx, dy), ha="center",
                va="bottom" if dy > 0 else "top", fontsize=mpl.rcParams["legend.fontsize"],
                color=RED, linespacing=1.15,
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", lw=.6, color=RED, shrinkA=0, shrinkB=3))

ax.set_xlabel("Lung cancer patients diagnosed 2019–2023 (county denominator)")
ax.set_ylabel("Received curative-intent treatment (%)")
ax.set_title("Curative-intent treatment varies between Finnish counties far more than\n"
             "random variation allows: 10 of 22 counties fall outside 95 % limits",
             loc="left")
ax.set_xlim(60, 1620); ax.set_ylim(12, 42)
ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="lower right", handlelength=1.8, borderpad=.2)
ax.text(.012, .035, "Each point = one wellbeing services county.  Åland excluded (no counts reported).",
        transform=ax.transAxes, fontsize=mpl.rcParams["xtick.labelsize"], color=GREY)
fs.set_frame(ax)
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig("funnel_curative_intent.png", dpi=300)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- 6. rank correlations
CTX = {"pop_65plus_pct": "Population aged 65+ (%)",
       "daily_smokers_pct": "Daily smokers (%)",
       "education_level_index": "Education level index",
       "km_to_university_hospital": "Distance to university hospital (km)",
       "lung_incidence_per_100k": "Lung cancer incidence per 100 000"}
rows = []
for col, lab in CTX.items():
    sub = dat[["share_pct", col]].dropna()
    r, p = stats.spearmanr(sub.share_pct, sub[col])
    n = len(sub)
    seZ = np.sqrt((1 + r ** 2 / 2) / (n - 3))            # Bonett & Wright (2000)
    lo, hi = np.tanh(np.arctanh(r) + np.array([-1, 1]) * stats.norm.isf(.025) * seZ)
    rows.append(dict(variable=lab, column=col, n=n, spearman_rho=r,
                     ci_low=lo, ci_high=hi, p_value=p))
corr = pd.DataFrame(rows).sort_values("spearman_rho")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- 7. outputs
keep = ["area_id", "county", "collaborative_area", "n", "x", "share_pct",
        "share_ci_low_pct", "share_ci_high_pct", "z", "p_exact", "p_exact_bh",
        "limit_band", "direction", "outside95_binomial", "outside95_adjusted",
        "excess_treated_per_year", "lcl95_pct", "ucl95_pct", "lcl998_pct", "ucl998_pct",
        "lcl95_adj_pct", "ucl95_adj_pct", "lcl998_adj_pct", "ucl998_adj_pct",
        "lung_no_treatment_record_pct", "lung_incidence_per_100k", "pop_65plus_pct",
        "daily_smokers_pct", "education_level_index", "low_income_rate_pct",
        "km_to_university_hospital"]
out = dat[keep].rename(columns={"n": "patients_n", "x": "curative_intent_n"})
out = out.sort_values("share_pct")
out.to_csv("county_table_analysis.csv", index=False)
corr.to_csv("rank_correlations.csv", index=False)

stat = dict(p0=p0, K=K, Q=Q, p_Q=p_Q, phi=phi, phi_w=phi_w, tau_pct=tau_pct,
            n_sum=int(n_sum), x_sum=int(x_sum), excluded=excluded,
            nat_n=int(nat.lung_patients_2019_2023_n), nat_x=int(nat.curative_intent_n))
pd.Series(stat).to_json("global_stats.json")
print(pd.Series(stat))
print(out[["county", "patients_n", "curative_intent_n", "share_pct", "p_exact",
           "limit_band", "excess_treated_per_year"]].to_string(index=False))
print(corr.to_string(index=False))

| | |

sum as the centre line instead ({100*p0_alt:.2f} %) {'leaves the set of counties outside the 95 % limits unchanged' if same else 'changes which counties fall outside the 95 % limits'}.

## 2. Is the variation larger than chance?

| Statistic | Value |
|---|---|
| Counties | {K} |
| Pearson Q = Σ z² (test of homogeneity) | **{Q:.1f}** on {K-1} df, *p* ≈ 10^{p_Q_log10:.0f} |
| Dispersion factor φ = Q/K | **{phi:.2f}** (1.0 = pure binomial) |
| Winsorised φ (Spiegelhalter, 10 % each tail) | **{phi_w:.2f}** — used to inflate the limits |
| Between-county SD on the share scale (DerSimonian–Laird τ) | **{tau_pct:.1f} pp** |

φ ≈ {phi:.0f} means the observed between-county variance is about {phi:.0f}× what independent binomial
sampling at a common {100*p0:.1f} % would give. The differences are real; the only question is what produces them.

## 3. Counties outside the limits

Shares are exact (Clopper–Pearson) CIs; *p* is a two-sided exact binomial test of the county count
against the national {100*p0:.2f} %; *q* is the Benjamini–Hochberg value across all {K} counties.

### Above the limits — more curative-intent treatment than the national share

{tbl(hi, False)}

### Below the limits — less curative-intent treatment than the national share

{tbl(lo, True)}

The last column is the arithmetic gap: (national share × county patients − observed treatments) ÷ 5 years.
Summed over the {len(lo)} low counties, **{abs(lo.excess_treated_per_year.sum()):.0f} patients a year**
would have had a curative-intent treatment record had those counties treated at the national share.

**Overdispersion-adjusted reading.** With limits widened by √φ = {infl:.2f}, only **Helsinki**
({hi.iloc[0].share_pct if hi.iloc[0].county=='Helsinki' else out.loc[out.county=='Helsinki','share_pct'].iat[0]:.1f} %,
n = {out.loc[out.county=='Helsinki','patients_n'].iat[0]:,}) lies outside. This is not a retraction of the
finding — the adjusted limits *absorb* the between-county differences into the null, so they answer a
different question: "is this county unusual **given** that counties differ this much?" The {int(dat.outside95_binomial.sum())}
counties outside the binomial limits are the ones that differ from the national average; Helsinki is the
one that is extreme even on the scale of the counties' own spread. Note that Vantaa and Kerava has the
highest share ({out.share_pct.max():.1f} %) but falls inside the adjusted limits because its denominator is
smaller than Helsinki's.

{corr_tbl}

Spearman ρ with Bonett–Wright 95 % CIs, n = {K} counties (Åland has context data but no share, so it is
excluded here too). **These are ecological associations between county aggregates, not causes.** With
{K} units the CIs are wide, the five variables are strongly intercorrelated with each other (older,
more peripheral counties are also the lower-education, higher-incidence ones), and nothing here identifies
an effect on an individual patient's chance of curative-intent treatment — the ecological fallacy applies
in full. No multiplicity adjustment is applied to these five tests; treat them as description, not inference.

population, shorter distance to a university hospital and higher education index have higher
curative-intent shares, and counties with high lung cancer incidence have lower shares. The five
university-hospital host counties and their neighbours (Helsinki, Vantaa and Kerava, Central and West
Uusimaa, Pirkanmaa) are the high group; Lapland, Kymenlaakso, South Karelia, Kainuu and North Karelia
the low group. Daily smoking is the one variable whose CI comfortably spans zero.

## 5. Limits of what these numbers can show

1. **Recording, not only treatment.** The registry's own quality report states that stage is recorded
   for roughly half of lung cancer patients and that recording practice differs between counties. The
   curative-intent share is conditioned on what reaches the registry, so an unknown part of the spread
   is documentation rather than care delivered.
2. **The no-treatment-record column points the same way.** `lung_no_treatment_record_pct` ranges from
   {out.lung_no_treatment_record_pct.min():.1f} % (Kymenlaakso) to {out.lung_no_treatment_record_pct.max():.1f} %
   (Southwest Finland) across counties — a {out.lung_no_treatment_record_pct.max()-out.lung_no_treatment_record_pct.min():.1f}
   pp spread in how often *any* treatment is recorded. A county can appear to have a low curative-intent
   share because treatment was given elsewhere or not captured. Southwest Finland and South Karelia, two
   low-share counties, have the two highest no-record shares (43.1 % and 42.8 %).
3. **No case-mix adjustment.** Stage, performance status, histology, age and comorbidity are the
   determinants of whether curative intent is even possible, and none is in this table. The funnel
   compares crude shares; a county with more advanced-stage or frailer patients should have a lower
   share for clinical reasons. Indirect standardisation was not possible with the data supplied.
4. **Referral across county borders.** Curative treatment is concentrated in university hospitals.
   Where a patient is treated and which county is credited need not coincide, which can move counts
   between neighbouring counties.
5. **Five pooled years.** 2019–2023 spans the COVID-19 period; the table gives no year breakdown, so
   no trend or disruption can be separated.
6. **Multiplicity.** With {K} simultaneous comparisons, BH-adjusted *q* values are reported alongside
   the raw exact *p* values; the 99.8 % limits serve the same purpose graphically.
7. **Åland** contributes nothing to this analysis — it has no reported counts, and that absence is
   reported rather than filled.

- [lung_curative_funnel.py](@@SCRIPT@@) — full analysis script
- [county_table_input.csv](@@INPUT@@) — the input table as supplied
"""

{"stdout":"# Curative-intent treatment of lung cancer across Finland's wellbeing services counties, 2019–2023

**Question.** Are between-county differences in the share of lung cancer patients receiving
curative-intent treatment larger than chance alone would produce, and which counties are genuine outliers?

**Answer.** Yes, decisively. The 22 counties with reported counts scatter about the national share
far beyond binomial sampling error (Q = 187.7 on 21 df, *p* ≈ 10^-28;
dispersion factor φ = 8.5, winsorised φ = 6.6). Shares run from
18.5 % to 35.6 % — a 17.2
percentage-point spread, against a national 27.0 %. Against plain binomial limits
12 of 22 counties are outside the 95 % limits
(7 outside 99.8 %); after inflating the limits by the
observed overdispersion, 1 county (Helsinki) remains outside.

![Funnel plot]({{artifact:91f56a8b-8394-4d32-9078-13a98aee567d}})

## 1. Rows used

| | |
|---|---|
| Counties analysed | **22** — every row with both counts (`area_id` 01–21 and 90) |
| Excluded | **Åland** (`area_id` 91): patients, curative-intent count, share and case count are all empty; nothing can be derived, so it enters no plot, test or correlation |
| Finland row (`area_id` FI) | used **only** as the centre line: 4,009/14,873 = 26.95 % |
| Denominator | `lung_patients_2019_2023_n` (registry report) |
| Numerator | `curative_intent_n` (registry report) |

**No count was derived from share × case count.** The second source's `lung_cases_5y_n` is identical to
`lung_patients_2019_2023_n` for all 22 counties, and the recomputed share `curative_intent_n / patients`
reproduces the reported `lung_curative_intent_pct` to within 0.05 pp everywhere, so the counts were used as given.

","stderr":"","exit_code":0}

    if s > h998 or s < l998: return "outside 99.8%"
    if s > h95 or s < l95:   return "outside 95%"
    return "within 95%"

    nn = row.n
    (l95, h95) = [a[0] for a in exact_limits(np.array([nn]), p0, ALPHA_IN)]
    (l998, h998) = [a[0] for a in exact_limits(np.array([nn]), p0, ALPHA_OUT)]
    s = row.x / nn
    return pd.Series({
        "band_binomial": band(s, l95, h95, l998, h998),
        "band_overdisp_adjusted": band(s, adj(l95), adj(h95), adj(l998), adj(h998)),
        "direction": "above" if s > p0 else "below",
        "lcl95_pct": 100 * l95, "ucl95_pct": 100 * h95,
        "lcl998_pct": 100 * l998, "ucl998_pct": 100 * h998,

dat["outside95_binomial"] = ~dat.band_binomial.eq("within 95%")

# Publication-Grade Figure Rules

*A checklist for correct, legible, internally-consistent scientific figures. This
skill does not impose a visual house style — frame, font, and palette are
parameters. Once loaded, call `apply_figure_style()` before plotting.*

## §0 Scope

**Load trigger** (same rule as the system prompt's "Publication-grade plots"
section): this skill is for **final-deliverable figures** — those shipping in a
report, paper, or export, or saved as an artifact the user will keep — not for
exploratory/intermediate plots (quick looks, EDA, sanity checks), which are
drawn plainly without it. Once loaded, "every plot" below means every plot you
render toward the deliverable.

§1–§3, §8, and §9 are **correctness** — they apply to every plot, in every
context, and have no aesthetic content. §4–§7 are **guidance** — defaults that
produce a clean result but that a deliberate alternative can override
(individual rules inside §4–§7 that state a factual/perceptual invariant — e.g.
§4.4 semantic-zero centering, §4.5 CVD, §6.9 leader anchoring — still bind). On
its own, this skill is the inner tier (make one plot good); `figure-composer`
and `paper-narrative` supply multi-panel and whole-paper context.

---

## §1 Data fidelity & self-consistency

**1.1 Excluded rows.** A row marked excluded or flagged in the source data is
either omitted entirely or drawn with a visually distinct open/hatched marker
and named in the key. It **never** enters a summary statistic plotted alongside
the included rows.

**1.2 Comparable conditions only.** Arms measured under non-comparable
conditions (different N, epoch budget, initialization, protocol) are not plotted
as visual peers. Separate them with a facet break or a marker on the label, and
state the difference once in the caption.

**1.3 Self-consistency.** Every key, threshold, and title inside the figure must
be satisfied by every plotted row. Before saving, walk each categorical outcome
label back to the rule that defines it; if a row's value contradicts its label
or the title, the figure is wrong, not the data.

**1.4 Claim-titles must be true.** A sentence-title (§5.1) is tested against
every category on the axis before rendering. If any contradicts it, qualify the
title ("on 3 of 4 pairs") or downgrade it to a description.

**1.5 State n and what was held fixed.** Every panel that draws a summary mark
states `n` and the unit of replication, and every small-multiple that holds a
variable fixed states the fixed value — in the panel or, when §2 budget is
tight, in the caption.

**1.6 Reference structure is reference.** A tree, ordering, or topology drawn as
*context* (a scale bar, a category strip) uses an established reference, not
one inferred from the plotted data. Infer the structure only when the structure
*is* the result.

**1.7 One number per claim.** A quantitative claim (runtime, accuracy, count)
has exactly one canonical value across every panel, caption, and the abstract.
Define what it measures and use that value everywhere.

---

## §2 Label economy — floor and ceiling

The figure shows the pattern; the **caption** carries the context. Design for a
general scientific reader, not the author.

**2.1 Floor (non-removable).** Every distinct mark, series, glyph, or comparator
must be identifiable from the figure alone. The caption explains *why it
matters*, not *what it is*. A label is non-removable if deleting it leaves a
reader asking "what is that?"; it is removable only if the question becomes "why
is that there?". Comparator labels name the thing ("prior method", "no joint
training"), never a bare role word ("baseline", "previous"). Any term a general
scientist can't parse gets a one-word gloss.

**2.2 Ceiling.** Per panel: title + axis labels + tick labels + series identity
(labeled once per row of small multiples) + at most 2–3 result annotations.
Count the strings; >6 beyond axes/ticks means you're over. The ceiling counts
*narrative* annotations (callouts, value labels, brackets) — identity labels are
floor, not budget.

**2.3 Move to the caption:** n=, what's-held-fixed, abbreviation expansions,
non-comparable footnotes, exclusion rationale, methodological caveats.

**2.4 Titles are takeaways.** A reader seeing only the title knows what the
panel shows. "Robust to gene dropout" passes; "Fewer genes" fails. Test: read it
aloud cold — if the listener asks "fewer genes *what*?", rewrite. For a row of
small multiples that vary one thing, drop per-panel titles for one row-header.

**2.5 Value-on-mark only for the headline number** — the one a reader would
quote. Everything else is read off the axis.

**2.6 When in doubt, delete the label and re-read.** If the message survives, it
stays deleted.

---

## §3 Axes, scales, small multiples

**3.1 Axis padding.** Axis limits clear the data by ≥ one marker radius on every
side; markers and text never touch a spine. `ax.margins(0.04)` after plotting,
or extend the limit past any annotation.

**3.2 Axis breaks over wasted range.** When data occupy <40 % of an axis, break
the axis or start it at the data floor with a clear non-zero tick. Never draw a
reference line, threshold, or annotation inside a broken-axis gap — the gap has
no coordinate.

**3.3 Log axes get human-readable ticks** — `10²`, `10³`, or `1k / 10k / 100k`,
not raw exponents. **Never** draw filled bars on a log-scaled value axis (bar
length encodes ratio to an arbitrary floor); use points + median tick instead.

**3.4 Shared axes across small multiples.** A row or column of small multiples
shows tick labels once (leftmost / bottommost panel); interior panels keep ticks
but drop labels. When the panels share a y-axis and differ only by x-variable,
render them as abutting subplots (`wspace≤0.06`) with one row-header title.

**3.5 Fill the box.** A panel's data envelope occupies ≥75 % of its allotted
rectangle. If a panel's natural aspect leaves dead bands, reshape the grid
(rowspan, stacked complementary panels) — don't pad the panel.

**3.6 Direction of goodness.** When higher- or lower-is-better is not obvious
from the axis label, place a small upright cue ("higher = better") in the
margin — once per row of panels, never per panel, and never only in the caption.
A directional glyph embedded in rotated text rotates with it; set the cue
upright.

**3.7 Physical width.** A single-row figure at 300 dpi fits the venue's
double-column width. Adding a schematic or labels does not push data panels narrower than
they were before.

---

## §4 Color

**4.1 Threading.** Once a color is bound to an entity (a method, a feature, a
condition), reuse that exact color for every mark representing that entity
across the figure — line, fill, marker, text, heatmap row. Color *is* the
cross-reference; a reader should never have to consult a legend twice.

**4.2 Limit hues.** Use as few distinct hues as the data require. When the
figure compares a focal series against others, make the focal series visually
dominant (saturated, heavier weight) and render comparators with lower visual
weight (desaturated, lighter, or thinner). The focal hue must not coincide with
any hue in a categorical palette used in the same figure. The focal series must
remain identifiable even when its mark is zero-width or coincident with others —
via outline, marker, or a light tinted band.

**4.3 Hierarchical categories.** When categories nest (groups within groups),
the outer level picks the hue family and the inner level samples within it.

**4.4 Continuous and diverging.** Use a perceptually uniform sequential map for
generic continuous values; a single-hue ramp for ordinal rank or size; a
diverging map for signed quantities — **always** centered at the semantically
meaningful zero (0, 1.0, or median), never the data midpoint.

**4.5 CVD safety.** Never rely on a red/green contrast for a binary or opposing
distinction. Any binary pair should remain distinguishable in deuteranopia
simulation. Reserve one alarm hue for error/anomaly/perturbation marks and do
not reuse it as a data-series color.

**4.6 Two palettes, two legends.** When a figure uses two categorical color
systems, each legend sits adjacent to the first panel where its palette applies.

---

## §5 Typography

**5.1 Sentence titles.** A panel title states the comparison in plain language,
regular weight, left-aligned. Metric names go on the axis, not in the title.

**5.2 Role-mapped size ladder.** A figure uses **at most three** font sizes,
mapped to *role* not space: titles/axis-labels/series-identity at the base size;
legend/annotation text one step down; tick labels one step further. Panel
letters are the only exception (bold, larger). If a label doesn't fit at its
role's size, fix the layout or shorten the text — don't reach for an
intermediate size. `apply_figure_style(sizes=(8,7,6))` sets the ladder.

**5.3 Nomenclature.** Species, gene, and variable names that scientific
convention italicizes are italicized. Abbreviated codes inherit the rule; expand
once on first appearance.

**5.4 Magnitude suffixes.** Large counts use `k / M / B` (`4.2B`, `120 kb`),
not comma-grouped full numerals.

**5.5 Numeric annotations.** On-mark numbers use at most 2 significant figures —
unless 2-sf rounding would make two distinct rows print the same value, in which
case show the digit that separates them. Text on a filled mark reaches ≥4.5:1
contrast; if it doesn't, place the text outside the mark.

**5.6 No internal codes.** Axis labels use plain-language names; codebase
abbreviations appear only in parentheses after the readable name or in the
caption. Comparator series are labeled with what they *are*, not a role word.

**5.7 Panel letters.** Bold, top-left, outside the axes box. Case follows the
target venue's convention; `panel_letter(ax, 'a', case=...)` handles either.

---

## §6 Chart-family guidance (by data shape)

**6.1 Categorical × numeric.** Show the distribution, not just the summary.
Chart choice follows n: jittered strip with a median tick for small n; box or
violin for large n; bar + overlaid raw points or bar + interval when the mean is
the message. The `errorbar='ci95'` interval is the t-distribution 95% CI of the
mean (half-width `t_{0.975,n−1}·s/√n`), so it is valid at small n. Error bars
and raw-point overlays are alternatives — showing both is usually redundant. A
category absent from a group is marked (`n.d.`, `—`, or a hatched ghost) at its
slot; an empty slot reads as zero. A zero-valued bar
gets a visible stub or dot at the baseline.

**6.2 Single-observation categories.** A filled dot with a thin neutral stem to
the semantic zero (lollipop). Value labels sit beside the dot.

**6.3 Continuous series.** Mean-per-x as a line with markers; individual runs as
thin translucent lines or points behind it. Label each series with direct text
at the right end of its line in preference to a legend box. Summary glyphs
(per-bin mean/median) use a shape that cannot be mistaken for a raw observation,
identical across series, drawn below the raw points in z-order.

**6.4 Distributions on shared support.** When two distributions overlap heavily,
stack them as small panels with a shared x-axis or use a ridgeline. Overlay only
when the separation is visually clear.

**6.5 Matrices.** When a heatmap is small enough to read (< ~200 cells), print
the value in every cell. State the threshold once in the colorbar label.

**6.6 Embeddings.** Dimensionality-reduction scatters (UMAP, t-SNE, PCA) drop
ticks and tick labels; a small corner arrow pair names the axes. Clusters are
labeled by thin leader lines to text in surrounding whitespace.

**6.7 Paired prediction vs. observation.** Stack the two as adjacent tracks with
identical x and color; let the alignment carry the comparison. Target regions
are translucent spans registered in the legend.

**6.8 Insets.** Connect a detail inset to its source region visibly — a bounding
box with connector lines, or a translucent wedge.

**6.9 Label the extremes.** On a scatter of named observations, direct-label at
least the maximum, minimum, and any flagged point with a thin leader line. After
rendering, verify every leader endpoint terminates within one marker radius of
the row it names.

---

## §7 Layout & narrative

**7.1 Show what is measured before the result.** A reader should grasp what's
being compared before seeing the comparison — via a plain-language title, a
labeled schematic, or panel ordering. Any schematic uses the same words and
glyphs as the data panels' labels.

**7.2 One figure, one message.** A multi-panel figure has a single sentence it
is trying to make true. Every panel either states it, supports it, or bounds it;
panels that do none of these belong in supplement.

**7.3 Legends live in whitespace.** Frameless, placed inside the figure's
natural whitespace, or replaced by direct labeling. Legend entries are
swatch-first, left-aligned, and resolve every visually distinct glyph on the
panel.

**7.4 Row-band headers for nested faceting.** When small multiples are grouped,
each group gets one spanning header, not repeated per-panel titles.

**7.5 The figure arc.** For a paper: Figure 1 renders the paper's one-sentence
pitch as data — scope, not architecture. Subsequent figures cover mechanism,
evidence, robustness, application. A panel is judged against the paper's pitch,
not just its own figure's claim; content moves between figures if that's where
the story needs it. (`paper-narrative` runs this review.)

**7.6 Don't re-decorate a passing panel.** Between revision rounds, a panel that
already passes is not made more visually complex to fix nothing. Adding marks or
labels to a clean panel is a regression.

---

## §8 Anti-patterns

These are correctness failures, not style preferences:

- Red and green as opposing categories.
- Filled bars on a log-scaled value axis.
- Colorbar ticks that are evenly spaced but miss the semantic center.
- A diverging colormap whose center is the data midpoint, not the semantic zero.
- An axis title that restates the tick labels.
- Explaining the direction of goodness only in the caption.
- A "reference" line drawn at a value that is itself one of the plotted points.
- An excluded row that enters a plotted summary statistic.
- A leader line whose nearest mark is not the row it labels.

---

## §9 Render-then-verify

After `fig.savefig(...)`, before `save_artifacts`:

**9.1 Geometric (bbox) check.**
```python
r = fig.canvas.get_renderer()
texts = [(t, t.get_window_extent(r)) for t in fig.findobj(mpl.text.Text)
         if t.get_text().strip() and t.get_visible()]
spines = [(s, s.get_window_extent(r)) for ax in fig.axes
          for s in ax.spines.values() if s.get_visible()]
ticklabels = {ax: set(ax.get_xticklabels(which='both') + ax.get_yticklabels(which='both'))
              for ax in fig.axes}
overlaps  = [(a, b) for i, (a, ba) in enumerate(texts) for b, bb in texts[i+1:] if ba.overlaps(bb)]
overlaps += [(t, s) for t, bt in texts for s, bs in spines
             if bt.overlaps(bs) and t not in ticklabels[s.axes]]
# assert: overlaps == [] and every text box lies within fig.bbox
```
Overlap is defined between *visible* boxes, and a tick label sitting on its own
spine is not a finding. Fix (move, shorten, stagger) and re-save until clean.

**9.2 Perceptual check.** The bbox check is geometric, not perceptual — it will
not catch a low-contrast label, a leader that crosses three others, or a series
color mistakable for another. Crop the saved PNG to each panel and look:
```python
fig.savefig("figure.png")
for letter, box in panel_crops(fig).items():
    host.view_image("figure.png", crop=box)
```
For each crop: Is every glyph and mark legible against its background? Does the
smallest plotted element have a stroke or stub? Do any leaders cross? Could any
series color be mistaken for another? Does the legend sit beside what it keys?
A perceptual defect that passes §9.1 is still a defect.

---
*When in doubt: fewer hues, more direct labels, raw data over summary stats, and
state what is being measured before showing the result.*

# Publication-Grade Figure Rules

*A checklist for correct, legible, internally-consistent scientific figures. This
skill does not impose a visual house style — frame, font, and palette are
parameters. Once loaded, call `apply_figure_style()` before plotting.*

## §0 Scope

**Load trigger** (same rule as the system prompt's "Publication-grade plots"
section): this skill is for **final-deliverable figures** — those shipping in a
report, paper, or export, or saved as an artifact the user will keep — not for
exploratory/intermediate plots (quick looks, EDA, sanity checks), which are
drawn plainly without it. Once loaded, "every plot" below means every plot you
render toward the deliverable.

§1–§3, §8, and §9 are **correctness** — they apply to every plot, in every
context, and have no aesthetic content. §4–§7 are **guidance** — defaults that
produce a clean result but that a deliberate alternative can override
(individual rules inside §4–§7 that state a factual/perceptual invariant — e.g.
§4.4 semantic-zero centering, §4.5 CVD, §6.9 leader anchoring — still bind). On
its own, this skill is the inner tier (make one plot good); `figure-composer`
and `paper-narrative` supply multi-panel and whole-paper context.

---

## §1 Data fidelity & self-consistency

**1.1 Excluded rows.** A row marked excluded or flagged in the source data is
either omitted entirely or drawn with a visually distinct open/hatched marker
and named in the key. It **never** enters a summary statistic plotted alongside
the included rows.

**1.2 Comparable conditions only.** Arms measured under non-comparable
conditions (different N, epoch budget, initialization, protocol) are not plotted
as visual peers. Separate them with a facet break or a marker on the label, and
state the difference once in the caption.

**1.3 Self-consistency.** Every key, threshold, and title inside the figure must
be satisfied by every plotted row. Before saving, walk each categorical outcome
label back to the rule that defines it; if a row's value contradicts its label
or the title, the figure is wrong, not the data.

**1.4 Claim-titles must be true.** A sentence-title (§5.1) is tested against
every category on the axis before rendering. If any contradicts it, qualify the
title ("on 3 of 4 pairs") or downgrade it to a description.

**1.5 State n and what was held fixed.** Every panel that draws a summary mark
states `n` and the unit of replication, and every small-multiple that holds a
variable fixed states the fixed value — in the panel or, when §2 budget is
tight, in the caption.

**1.6 Reference structure is reference.** A tree, ordering, or topology drawn as
*context* (a scale bar, a category strip) uses an established reference, not
one inferred from the plotted data. Infer the structure only when the structure
*is* the result.

**1.7 One number per claim.** A quantitative claim (runtime, accuracy, count)
has exactly one canonical value across every panel, caption, and the abstract.
Define what it measures and use that value everywhere.

---

## §2 Label economy — floor and ceiling

The figure shows the pattern; the **caption** carries the context. Design for a
general scientific reader, not the author.

**2.1 Floor (non-removable).** Every distinct mark, series, glyph, or comparator
must be identifiable from the figure alone. The caption explains *why it
matters*, not *what it is*. A label is non-removable if deleting it leaves a
reader asking "what is that?"; it is removable only if the question becomes "why
is that there?". Comparator labels name the thing ("prior method", "no joint
training"), never a bare role word ("baseline", "previous"). Any term a general
scientist can't parse gets a one-word gloss.

**2.2 Ceiling.** Per panel: title + axis labels + tick labels + series identity
(labeled once per row of small multiples) + at most 2–3 result annotations.
Count the strings; >6 beyond axes/ticks means you're over. The ceiling counts
*narrative* annotations (callouts, value labels, brackets) — identity labels are
floor, not budget.

**2.3 Move to the caption:** n=, what's-held-fixed, abbreviation expansions,
non-comparable footnotes, exclusion rationale, methodological caveats.

**2.4 Titles are takeaways.** A reader seeing only the title knows what the
panel shows. "Robust to gene dropout" passes; "Fewer genes" fails. Test: read it
aloud cold — if the listener asks "fewer genes *what*?", rewrite. For a row of
small multiples that vary one thing, drop per-panel titles for one row-header.

**2.5 Value-on-mark only for the headline number** — the one a reader would
quote. Everything else is read off the axis.

**2.6 When in doubt, delete the label and re-read.** If the message survives, it
stays deleted.

---

## §3 Axes, scales, small multiples

**3.1 Axis padding.** Axis limits clear the data by ≥ one marker radius on every
side; markers and text never touch a spine. `ax.margins(0.04)` after plotting,
or extend the limit past any annotation.

**3.2 Axis breaks over wasted range.** When data occupy <40 % of an axis, break
the axis or start it at the data floor with a clear non-zero tick. Never draw a
reference line, threshold, or annotation inside a broken-axis gap — the gap has
no coordinate.

**3.3 Log axes get human-readable ticks** — `10²`, `10³`, or `1k / 10k / 100k`,
not raw exponents. **Never** draw filled bars on a log-scaled value axis (bar
length encodes ratio to an arbitrary floor); use points + median tick instead.

**3.4 Shared axes across small multiples.** A row or column of small multiples
shows tick labels once (leftmost / bottommost panel); interior panels keep ticks
but drop labels. When the panels share a y-axis and differ only by x-variable,
render them as abutting subplots (`wspace≤0.06`) with one row-header title.

**3.5 Fill the box.** A panel's data envelope occupies ≥75 % of its allotted
rectangle. If a panel's natural aspect leaves dead bands, reshape the grid
(rowspan, stacked complementary panels) — don't pad the panel.

**3.6 Direction of goodness.** When higher- or lower-is-better is not obvious
from the axis label, place a small upright cue ("higher = better") in the
margin — once per row of panels, never per panel, and never only in the caption.
A directional glyph embedded in rotated text rotates with it; set the cue
upright.

**3.7 Physical width.** A single-row figure at 300 dpi fits the venue's
double-column width. Adding a schematic or labels does not push data panels narrower than
they were before.

---

## §4 Color

**4.1 Threading.** Once a color is bound to an entity (a method, a feature, a
condition), reuse that exact color for every mark representing that entity
across the figure — line, fill, marker, text, heatmap row. Color *is* the
cross-reference; a reader should never have to consult a legend twice.

**4.2 Limit hues.** Use as few distinct hues as the data require. When the
figure compares a focal series against others, make the focal series visually
dominant (saturated, heavier weight) and render comparators with lower visual
weight (desaturated, lighter, or thinner). The focal hue must not coincide with
any hue in a categorical palette used in the same figure. The focal series must
remain identifiable even when its mark is zero-width or coincident with others —
via outline, marker, or a light tinted band.

**4.3 Hierarchical categories.** When categories nest (groups within groups),
the outer level picks the hue family and the inner level samples within it.

**4.4 Continuous and diverging.** Use a perceptually uniform sequential map for
generic continuous values; a single-hue ramp for ordinal rank or size; a
diverging map for signed quantities — **always** centered at the semantically
meaningful zero (0, 1.0, or median), never the data midpoint.

**4.5 CVD safety.** Never rely on a red/green contrast for a binary or opposing
distinction. Any binary pair should remain distinguishable in deuteranopia
simulation. Reserve one alarm hue for error/anomaly/perturbation marks and do
not reuse it as a data-series color.

**4.6 Two palettes, two legends.** When a figure uses two categorical color
systems, each legend sits adjacent to the first panel where its palette applies.

---

## §5 Typography

**5.1 Sentence titles.** A panel title states the comparison in plain language,
regular weight, left-aligned. Metric names go on the axis, not in the title.

**5.2 Role-mapped size ladder.** A figure uses **at most three** font sizes,
mapped to *role* not space: titles/axis-labels/series-identity at the base size;
legend/annotation text one step down; tick labels one step further. Panel
letters are the only exception (bold, larger). If a label doesn't fit at its
role's size, fix the layout or shorten the text — don't reach for an
intermediate size. `apply_figure_style(sizes=(8,7,6))` sets the ladder.

**5.3 Nomenclature.** Species, gene, and variable names that scientific
convention italicizes are italicized. Abbreviated codes inherit the rule; expand
once on first appearance.

**5.4 Magnitude suffixes.** Large counts use `k / M / B` (`4.2B`, `120 kb`),
not comma-grouped full numerals.

**5.5 Numeric annotations.** On-mark numbers use at most 2 significant figures —
unless 2-sf rounding would make two distinct rows print the same value, in which
case show the digit that separates them. Text on a filled mark reaches ≥4.5:1
contrast; if it doesn't, place the text outside the mark.

**5.6 No internal codes.** Axis labels use plain-language names; codebase
abbreviations appear only in parentheses after the readable name or in the
caption. Comparator series are labeled with what they *are*, not a role word.

**5.7 Panel letters.** Bold, top-left, outside the axes box. Case follows the
target venue's convention; `panel_letter(ax, 'a', case=...)` handles either.

---

## §6 Chart-family guidance (by data shape)

**6.1 Categorical × numeric.** Show the distribution, not just the summary.
Chart choice follows n: jittered strip with a median tick for small n; box or
violin for large n; bar + overlaid raw points or bar + interval when the mean is
the message. The `errorbar='ci95'` interval is the t-distribution 95% CI of the
mean (half-width `t_{0.975,n−1}·s/√n`), so it is valid at small n. Error bars
and raw-point overlays are alternatives — showing both is usually redundant. A
category absent from a group is marked (`n.d.`, `—`, or a hatched ghost) at its
slot; an empty slot reads as zero. A zero-valued bar
gets a visible stub or dot at the baseline.

**6.2 Single-observation categories.** A filled dot with a thin neutral stem to
the semantic zero (lollipop). Value labels sit beside the dot.

**6.3 Continuous series.** Mean-per-x as a line with markers; individual runs as
thin translucent lines or points behind it. Label each series with direct text
at the right end of its line in preference to a legend box. Summary glyphs
(per-bin mean/median) use a shape that cannot be mistaken for a raw observation,
identical across series, drawn below the raw points in z-order.

**6.4 Distributions on shared support.** When two distributions overlap heavily,
stack them as small panels with a shared x-axis or use a ridgeline. Overlay only
when the separation is visually clear.

**6.5 Matrices.** When a heatmap is small enough to read (< ~200 cells), print
the value in every cell. State the threshold once in the colorbar label.

**6.6 Embeddings.** Dimensionality-reduction scatters (UMAP, t-SNE, PCA) drop
ticks and tick labels; a small corner arrow pair names the axes. Clusters are
labeled by thin leader lines to text in surrounding whitespace.

**6.7 Paired prediction vs. observation.** Stack the two as adjacent tracks with
identical x and color; let the alignment carry the comparison. Target regions
are translucent spans registered in the legend.

**6.8 Insets.** Connect a detail inset to its source region visibly — a bounding
box with connector lines, or a translucent wedge.

**6.9 Label the extremes.** On a scatter of named observations, direct-label at
least the maximum, minimum, and any flagged point with a thin leader line. After
rendering, verify every leader endpoint terminates within one marker radius of
the row it names.

---

## §7 Layout & narrative

**7.1 Show what is measured before the result.** A reader should grasp what's
being compared before seeing the comparison — via a plain-language title, a
labeled schematic, or panel ordering. Any schematic uses the same words and
glyphs as the data panels' labels.

**7.2 One figure, one message.** A multi-panel figure has a single sentence it
is trying to make true. Every panel either states it, supports it, or bounds it;
panels that do none of these belong in supplement.

**7.3 Legends live in whitespace.** Frameless, placed inside the figure's
natural whitespace, or replaced by direct labeling. Legend entries are
swatch-first, left-aligned, and resolve every visually distinct glyph on the
panel.

**7.4 Row-band headers for nested faceting.** When small multiples are grouped,
each group gets one spanning header, not repeated per-panel titles.

**7.5 The figure arc.** For a paper: Figure 1 renders the paper's one-sentence
pitch as data — scope, not architecture. Subsequent figures cover mechanism,
evidence, robustness, application. A panel is judged against the paper's pitch,
not just its own figure's claim; content moves between figures if that's where
the story needs it. (`paper-narrative` runs this review.)

**7.6 Don't re-decorate a passing panel.** Between revision rounds, a panel that
already passes is not made more visually complex to fix nothing. Adding marks or
labels to a clean panel is a regression.

---

## §8 Anti-patterns

These are correctness failures, not style preferences:

- Red and green as opposing categories.
- Filled bars on a log-scaled value axis.
- Colorbar ticks that are evenly spaced but miss the semantic center.
- A diverging colormap whose center is the data midpoint, not the semantic zero.
- An axis title that restates the tick labels.
- Explaining the direction of goodness only in the caption.
- A "reference" line drawn at a value that is itself one of the plotted points.
- An excluded row that enters a plotted summary statistic.
- A leader line whose nearest mark is not the row it labels.

---

## §9 Render-then-verify

After `fig.savefig(...)`, before `save_artifacts`:

**9.1 Geometric (bbox) check.**
```python
r = fig.canvas.get_renderer()
texts = [(t, t.get_window_extent(r)) for t in fig.findobj(mpl.text.Text)
         if t.get_text().strip() and t.get_visible()]
spines = [(s, s.get_window_extent(r)) for ax in fig.axes
          for s in ax.spines.values() if s.get_visible()]
ticklabels = {ax: set(ax.get_xticklabels(which='both') + ax.get_yticklabels(which='both'))
              for ax in fig.axes}
overlaps  = [(a, b) for i, (a, ba) in enumerate(texts) for b, bb in texts[i+1:] if ba.overlaps(bb)]
overlaps += [(t, s) for t, bt in texts for s, bs in spines
             if bt.overlaps(bs) and t not in ticklabels[s.axes]]
# assert: overlaps == [] and every text box lies within fig.bbox
```
Overlap is defined between *visible* boxes, and a tick label sitting on its own

import numpy as np
from scipy import special, optimize, stats

p0 = 4009/14873  # national line used in script? Actually script uses nat.curative_intent_n/nat.lung_patients_2019_2023_n
print("p0", p0)
phi_w = 6.642536
infl = np.sqrt(phi_w)
print("infl", infl)

def exact_limits_single(n, p, alpha):
    f = lambda k, targ: special.betainc(n - k, k + 1, 1 - p) - targ
    lo = optimize.brentq(f, 1e-9, n-1e-9, args=(alpha/2,)) / n
    hi = optimize.brentq(f, 1e-9, n-1e-9, args=(1-alpha/2,)) / n
    return lo, hi

for name, n, share in [("Vantaa and Kerava", 595, 35.630252), ("Helsinki", 1486, 33.041723), ("Central Uusimaa", 481, 33.679834), ("West Uusimaa", 1058, 31.852552), ("Pirkanmaa", 1253, 31.923384)]:
    lo95, hi95 = exact_limits_single(n, p0, 0.05)
    adj_hi = p0 + infl*(hi95-p0)
    adj_lo = p0 + infl*(lo95-p0)
    print(name, "share%", share, "adj_hi95%", adj_hi*100, "outside_adj?", share/100 > adj_hi)

**Rank correlations (exploratory, n = 22, Spearman with Bonett–Wright CIs):** 65+ share ρ = −0.77 (−0.91, −0.47); distance to university hospital −0.66 (−0.86, −0.30); lung cancer incidence −0.62 (−0.84, −0.24); education index +0.49 (+0.06, +0.77); daily smoking −0.30 (−0.65, +0.15). **Yes — the between-county differences are far larger than chance.** Homogeneity test on the 22 counties with counts: Q = 187.7 on 21 df, p ≈ 10⁻²⁸, dispersion factor φ = 8.5 (winsorised 6.6), between-county SD τ = 4.9 pp. Shares run 18.5 % → 35.6 % around a national 27.0 %.

![Funnel plot of curative-intent treatment share by county]({{artifact:91f56a8b-8394-4d32-9078-13a98aee567d}})

**Rows used.** All 22 counties that carry both counts (`area_id` 01–21, 90). Åland (`area_id` 91) has patients, curative-intent count, share and case count all empty — nothing is derivable, so it is excluded everywhere, including the correlations. **No count had to be derived from share × case count:** `lung_cases_5y_n` equals `lung_patients_2019_2023_n` for all 22, and the recomputed shares reproduce the reported ones to ≤0.05 pp. The Finland row is used only as the centre line (4,009/14,873 = 26.95 %). The 22 counties sum to 14,774 patients and 3,992 treatments, so 99 patients and 17 treatments sit in the national total but in no county row; using the 22-county sum (27.02 %) as the centre line instead leaves the set of flagged counties unchanged.

**Outliers (exact two-sided binomial vs 26.95 %, BH q across 22 tests).**

| Above | n | treated | share | p | q |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Vantaa and Kerava | 595 | 212 | 35.6 % | 3.6e-06 | 2.6e-05 |
| Central Uusimaa | 481 | 162 | 33.7 % | 0.0012 | 0.0033 |
| Helsinki | 1,486 | 491 | 33.0 % | 2.2e-07 | 2.4e-06 |
| Pirkanmaa | 1,253 | 400 | 31.9 % | 1.0e-04 | 4.4e-04 |
| West Uusimaa | 1,058 | 337 | 31.9 % | 4.1e-04 | 0.0015 |

| Below | n | treated | share | p | q | shortfall, patients/yr |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Lapland | 710 | 131 | 18.5 % | 1.4e-07 | 2.4e-06 | 12.1 |
| South Karelia | 355 | 67 | 18.9 % | 5.0e-04 | 0.0016 | 5.7 |
| Kymenlaakso | 591 | 114 | 19.3 % | 1.6e-05 | 8.6e-05 | 9.1 |
| Kainuu | 226 | 47 | 20.8 % | 0.0359 | 0.0659 | 2.8 |
| North Karelia | 510 | 109 | 21.4 % | 0.0044 | 0.0107 | 5.7 |
| North Ostrobothnia | 1,050 | 248 | 23.6 % | 0.0149 | 0.0327 | 7.0 |
| Southwest Finland | 1,437 | 349 | 24.3 % | 0.0221 | 0.0442 | 7.7 |

All five high counties and Lapland, South Karelia, Kymenlaakso are outside the 99.8 % limits; the other four low counties are between the 95 % and 99.8 % limits, and Kainuu is the only one that loses significance after FDR adjustment (q = 0.066). Together the seven low counties are about **50 patients a year** short of the national share.

With limits inflated by √φ = 2.58, only Helsinki stays outside — the adjusted limits absorb the county-level spread into the null, so they test "unusual *given* that counties differ this much", not whether the counties differ. Vantaa and Kerava has the highest share but falls inside the adjusted band because its denominator is smaller than Helsinki's.

**Rank correlations (exploratory, n = 22, Spearman with Bonett–Wright CIs):** 65+ share ρ = −0.77 (−0.91, −0.47); distance to university hospital −0.66 (−0.86, −0.30); lung cancer incidence −0.62 (−0.84, −0.24); education index +0.49 (+0.06, +0.77); daily smoking −0.30 (−0.65, +0.15). These are ecological associations between county aggregates, not causes — the five variables are strongly intercorrelated, the CIs are wide at 22 units, and none of this identifies an effect on an individual patient's chance of curative-intent treatment.

**Limits.** The registry reports stage for roughly half of lung cancer patients with county-varying recording practice, so part of the spread is documentation rather than care. The `lung_no_treatment_record_pct` column supports that reading: it ranges 16.4 % to 43.1 %, and Southwest Finland (43.1 %) and South Karelia (42.8 %), both low-share counties, hold the two highest values. There is no case-mix adjustment available (no stage, performance status, histology or comorbidity in the table), cross-county referral to university hospitals can move counts between neighbours, and the five pooled years span COVID-19 with no annual breakdown. Full caveats are in §5 of the summary.
